candidates.source_title: Killer who hid wife’s body under bed is jailed for life - Rochdale Times
candidates.source_body_excerpt: A man who murdered his wife and hid her body under a bed for two days has been jailed for a minimum of 21 years and six months. Kyle Howard, 36, of Tweedale Street, was sentenced today at Manchester Crown Court. Police found the body of Keeley Aspinall, 44, known as Kiki, on May 25 at their flat on the Freehold Estate. Howard told police he had fatally stabbed Keeley two days earlier and was reporting the incident because her body was beginning to smell. When questioned, Howard said that the pair had been drinking and began to argue in the kitchen. Keeley was cooking at the time and had a knife in her hand as the pair began to “tussle”. Howard admitted he had his hands around Keeley’s neck and punched her, but he could not remember exactly how the knife ended up in Keeley’s chest, but he said it “just did”. A Home Office post-mortem exmination found that Keeley had suffered a stab wound to the chest, bruising to her neck consistent with strangulation and various other scratches and bruises on her body. Throughout the investigation, Greater Manchester Police’s Major Incident Team unravelled a pattern of domestic abuse from Howard toward Keeley.
candidates.source_summary: A man who murdered his wife and hid her body under a bed for two days has been jailed for 21 years and six months.

candidates.source_body_excerpt: Police have asked parents to speak to their children and said they will 'invite parents to the police station' due to a town centre being plagued by large group of youths. The request, sent out by Greater Manchester Police (GMP) on Facebook, says that Heywood Town Centre in Rochdale has been suffering from issues with a large group of youths. These young people have been causing criminal damage, theft, assaults, and have been behaving in a 'generally intimidating' way. In an effort to combat the behaviour, GMP is inviting parents of the youths to the police station to make them aware of their children's behaviour. Police say they have identified the children from personal interactions and from reviewing CCTV via schools and other partner agencies. GMP added that Criminal Behaviour Orders may be put in place for these youths if things continue. A statement from GMP said: "Parents, please speak to your children. candidates.source_title: Young guitar star reaches national finals - Rochdale Times
candidates.source_body_excerpt: A young guitarist from Middleton will be taking on musicians twice his age after reaching the finals of a national competition. Nine-year-old Adrian Abraham took up the guitar two years ago but has now a finalist in the Under 18s category for the Undiscovered Talent UK (UTUK) National Talent Competition 2027. He is also on the verge of becoming a world record holder as the youngest person to pass the Grade 8 rock and pop guitar exam. Following a public vote, Adrian has officially been confirmed as a grand finalist for the competition which will be held at Stanley Arts in London in March. Adrian’s dad, Abraham, said: “Reaching the national finals at just nine years old is a deeply meaningful moment for Adrian, representing far more than a competition milestone. “When Adrian first picked up full-sized electric guitars, his small hand scale presented significant physical hurdles that made standard fretting and stretching an uphill battle. candidates.source_title: The sun sets on Rochdale's Seven Sisters
candidates.source_body_excerpt: The sun appears to be setting on the famous Seven Sisters tower blocks in Rochdale . On Monday, Rochdale Boroughwide Housing (RBH) announced their intention to demolish the goliaths that have dominated the town’s skyline since the 1960s . They want to replace the 766 flats, most of which sit empty, with 601 new homes. The scheme would provide a mix of flats and townhouses - with a shift towards more family homes from a setup of mainly bedsits and one-beds. The Seven Sisters - actually named College Bank - have become part of the furniture. Lots of Rochdalians having either lived there, or had friends and family live there. But it only takes one trip around the estate to realise the blocks have gotten into a sorry state. The garages below are all boarded up, rubbish is littered outside and the tower blocks themselves are becoming tatty, with signs visibly falling apart. RBH, who own the land, say they are becoming more unsafe - which is why two blocks have already been closed and the rest are currently being emptied. The decision to rehouse all 229 flats left occupied was made in October 2025 . Only 78 households remain, but they’re due to be out by next summer. Of those still left, there is a strong contingent of campaigners hoping to stop the demolition. The Save the Seven Sisters group (ST7S) want to see the blocks refurbished instead and have even come up with a plan on how to do it, but RBH don’t agree it’s feasible. Tenants have lived in limbo for a decade - ever since RBH originally announced their intention to demolish 10 years ago. RBH has shifted its stance multiple times - moving from part-demolition, to ruling it out entirely in 2023, before putting ‘all options back on the table’ in 2024, then finally deciding to demolish them this week. It has been a turbulent time to say the least. It could be argued that the situation is no further on than 10 years ago, but the picture in Rochdale has dramatically changed since. Former Greater Manchester mayor Andy Burnham put together a taskforce in 2024 to look into alternatives to demolition. The taskforce is made up of Rochdale council , the Greater Manchester Combined Authority (GMCA), the Rochdale MPs office, the Greater Manchester Tenants Union and RBH. The social housing provider says they have conducted surveys that suggest there are a number of structural issues with the blocks - which is the reason two of the blocks are currently out of action. In conjunction with the taskforce, RBH have costed up options for various forms of refurbishments and also demolition. Following a year-long review of those findings, the decision was finally made. RBH deemed it too expensive and believed it would take too long to refurbish the blocks, so opted to redevelop. They estimated that it would take 12 years to refurbish and cost £269m – around £388,000 per flat. Then, even after that, homes would have an expected lifespan of around 50 years, according to RBH. candidates.source_title: Organised crime gang ‘manager’ jailed for supplying class-A drugs - Rochdale Times
candidates.source_body_excerpt: A man who played a significant role in an organised crime group which supplied class A drugs across Rochdale has been jailed for 10 years and six months. An investigation into Haider Ali was launched following information received that a drug deal had taken place from a car parked in Baron Street, in Rochdale town centre, just before midnight on January 4, 2025. Officers began to follow the vehicle and when it came to a stop at a local petrol station, officers immediately executed a reinforced stop to prevent it from making off. Ali, who was travelling as a passenger, exited the vehicle and began to speedily walk away before officers detained him. Following searches, Ali was found to be in possession of more than £1,000 in cash, and two mobile phones, all of which were seized. Ali was arrested on suspicion of being concerned in the supply of class A drugs and taken to custody where further searches recovered two bundles of several wraps of a brown and a white substance. Tests later confirmed these substances to be heroin and cocaine. A pre-paid mobile phone seized from Ali was confirmed to be the Adam drug line. Following this, investigators also uncovered that Ali was not only dealing drugs at street level, but he was also managing other street dealers. Evidence suggested that Ali had progressed from being a street dealer in 2014 to holding a significant role within the Adam OCG in 2024 into 2025, managing street dealers and the dedicated dealer phone, and directing those below him on where there next deal is.

Ahmed - known by his victims as 'Daddy' - was sentenced to 19 years in prison at Liverpool Crown Court in 2012 as one of nine men convicted of offences against five girls. He was released in July after serving 14 years. In a situation that has caused a diplomatic row, the 73-year-old can't be deported because of a 1971 law applying to Commonwealth citizens who arrived in the UK more than 50 years ago. It is being called a 'loophole'. Click here to get the biggest stories straight to your inbox in our Daily Newsletter Ahmed has been stripped of his British citizenship, leaving him solely as a Pakistani national. Following his release, Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said her intention was to change the legal loophole to make it possible to deport those convicted of serious crimes , including terrorism and child sexual exploitation. Pakistan has insisted it will not accept Ahmed's return. Ms Mahmood said the government was preparing to bring forward an ammendment to The Immigration and Asylum Bill because of the case of Ahmed. It went through its third reading in the House of Commons on Tuesday (November 17) and passed by 290 votes to 94. It will now progress to the House of Lords for scrutiny. Sky News interviewed 'Angelina' - not her real name - who told how she was raped by Ahmed as a teenager. She recalled going to a hospital after one attack, but said she was left with 'no support'. "They left me like I was an aninal in the world that you leave in a cage," she said. Ahmed, it is understood, is prevented from being in Rochdale and Greater Manchester as part of his release on licence arrangements. But Angelina said she fears he's been placed 'close' to where she lives. "That's the fear that I have," she said. She said she's now been accepted onto a list to relocate 200 miles away. candidates.source_body_excerpt: A school where staff took industrial action over concerns about safety has been put into special measures after Ofsted inspectors found “harmful behaviours have become normalised”. Union members at St Cuthbert’s RC High School took strike action between February and June in a dispute with St Teresa of Calcutta Catholic Academy Trust which runs the school. Following an inspection which took place on October 6, His Majesty’s Chief Inspector found that urgent improvement is required — the lowest of the new inspection rankings — as it put the school into special measures. The report said the school is “failing to provide an acceptable standard of education, and the persons responsible for leading, managing or governing the school are not demonstrating the capacity to secure the necessary improvement in the school”. Inspectors noted that St Cuthbert’s has undergone a significant change since the last inspection, with four headteachers and an interim executive headteacher who has been in post since November, 2025. The governing body has been disbanded and has been replaced by a trust intervention committee. Following the visit, inspectors found that safeguarding standards have not been met. Their report said: “Leaders have not ensured that there is an open and positive culture around safeguarding that adequately protects pupils from harm. NASUWT members on strike at St Cuthbert’s. candidates.source_title: This Rochdale roast dinner has been named one of the best in the UK - Oldham Times
candidates.source_body_excerpt: One of the best Sunday roasts in the country can be found in Rochdale, according to a new ranking. The Good Food Guide has released its list of the top 40 roasts in the UK, which includes the Martlet in Rochdale town centre. The Martlet opened inside the grand town hall in September 2024, just a few months after the Grade I-listed building reopened to the public following extensive refurbishments. In its review of the restaurant, the Good Food Guide praised the menu’s “sturdy simplicity” and “pride in local produce and tradition”. It said: “Concealed within the Victorian Gothic grandeur of Rochdale Town Hall, the Martlet Kitchen (named after a mythical local bird with no feet) is a fine riposte to decades of negative public image. “Any doubts about operating in a civic setting, however, are swept away by the quality of the food.” The reviewer highlighted menu items such as the “sell-out” pies, as well as more “culturally diverse” items such as coriander bhajis and rigatoni with meatballs. As for the roast dinners, the review said they were as “equally traditional” as the rest of the menu, and mentioned the “roast sirloin of Cheshire beef or garlicky, minty leg of Dales lamb with all the trimmings”.
